links.outcome: Hallucination rate with RAG on curated CIS source versus Google-based RAG versus no RAG
links.effect: Hallucination rates 0% (GPT-4) and 6% (GPT-3.5) with CIS RAG; conventional chatbots about 40%. OR vs CIS: Google 9.4 (95% CI 1.2-17.5), conventional 16.1 (95% CI 3.7-50.0).
links.quote: Similarly, conventional GPTs had an OR of 16.1 (95% CI 3.7‐50.0; P <.001) compared to those with RAG reference data from CIS.

links.outcome: Effect of vetted versus unvetted retrieval corpus on hallucination rate
links.effect: Google-retrieval chatbots had 18% hallucinations among answered questions vs 2% for CIS chatbots; Google OR 9.4 (95% CI 1.2-17.5, P<.01) versus CIS.
links.quote: In multivariate analysis, adjusting for other factors, models with RAG reference data from Google search results were more likely to generate hallucinations compared with those with RAG reference data from CIS, with an OR of 9.4 (95% CI 1.2‐17.5; P <.01).

links.outcome: Ability to decline to answer when information lacking, versus always responding
links.effect: Conventional chatbots responded to 100% of questions; RAG chatbots response rate fell to 36-81%. CIS chatbots gave 0% response for questions not covered by CIS.
links.quote: The chatbots with RAG (ie, CIS chatbot and Google chatbot) had lower response rates than the conventional models.

links.outcome: Hallucination rate of conventional GPT chatbots on cancer questions against reference review
links.effect: Conventional GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 generated hallucinations in 37% and 40% of responses respectively.
links.quote: The conventional models generated hallucinations in approximately 40% of their responses.
